senses.definition: To drive a hackney cab.
senses.example: After losing his job at the plant, he hacked around the city for years.

senses.definition: To cough noisily.
senses.example: This cold is awful. I can't stop hacking.

senses.definition: To play hackeysack.
senses.example: Every afternoon the students hacked in the quad, kicking the little beanbag between them.

senses.definition: To swing at a pitched ball.
senses.example: He went to the batter's box hacking.

senses.definition: (dated) To make common or cliched; to vulgarise.
senses.example: Some critics felt the poet had hacked his sonnets into greeting-card sentiment.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A tool for chopping.
senses.example: He sharpened the hack and went to clear the brush behind the barn.

senses.definition: A hacking blow.
senses.example: A single hack from the axe split the log cleanly down the middle.

senses.definition: A gouge or notch made by such a blow.
senses.example: The bark on the oak still bore a deep hack where the logger had struck.

senses.definition: A try, an attempt.
senses.example: I'll give the crossword one more hack before I look up the answers.

senses.definition: The foothold traditionally cut into the ice from which the person who throws the rock pushes off for delivery.
senses.example: The skip pointed out the hack, where the thrower would push off for the stone.

senses.definition: An improvised device or solution to a problem.
An expedient, temporary solution, such as a small patch or change to code, meant to be replaced with a more elegant solution at a later date; a workaround.
senses.example: Valleysoft released a hack yesterday to fix the "crashes when more than 50 recipients" bug for people who need it right away. The company says its next release will also solve this as well as add new features.

senses.definition: An interesting technical achievement, particularly in computer programming.
senses.example: Flugensoft came out with a neat hack last week that allows your watch to warm up your car if it's below freezing outside.

senses.definition: A trick, shortcut, skill, or novel method to increase productivity, efficiency, or ease.
senses.example: Putting your phone in a sandwich bag when you go to the beach is such a great hack.

senses.definition: The illegal accessing of a computer network.
A video game or any computer software that has been altered from its original state.
A practical joke that showcases cleverness and creativity.
The act of striking an opponent with one's hockey stick, typically on the leg but occasionally and more seriously on the back, arm, head, etc.
senses.example: Zersky is still down after that nasty hack by Lenner.

senses.definition: A kick on the shins in football of any type.
senses.example: Wales are awarded a free kick after a minor hack by Järvinen on Llewellyn.

senses.definition: Confinement of an officer to their stateroom as a punishment.
A board upon which the falcon's food is placed; used by extension for the state of partial freedom in which they are kept before being trained.
A food-rack for cattle.
A rack used to dry something, such as bricks, fish, or cheese.
A grating in a mill race.
A horse for hire, especially one which is old and tired.
A person, often a journalist, hired to do routine work.
senses.example: I got by on hack work for years before I finally published my novel.

senses.definition: Someone who is available for hire; hireling, mercenary.
The driver of a taxicab (hackney cab).
A vehicle let for hire; originally, a hackney cab, now typically a taxicab.
A hearse.
An untalented writer.
senses.example: Dason is nothing but a two-bit hack.

senses.definition: One who is professionally successful despite producing mediocre work. (Usually applied to persons in a creative field.)
A talented writer-for-hire, paid to put others' thoughts into felicitous language.
A political agitator.
A dry cough.
A hacking; a catch in speaking; a short, broken cough.
A small ball usually made of woven cotton or suede and filled with rice, sand or some other filler, for use in hackeysack.
Time check, as for example upon synchronization of wristwatches.
senses.example: Related terms: hack watch

senses.definition: A swing of the bat at a pitched ball by the batter, particularly a choppy, ungraceful one that misses the ball such as at a fastball.
senses.example: And Melnick goes down with one last hack at an O'Malley fastball.

senses.definition: An airplane of poor quality or in poor condition.
(dated) A computer programmer who makes quick but inelegant changes to computer code to solve problems or add features.
senses.example: Tsang is great but Zhou is such a hack — I wouldn't want him on my project.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A computer programmer, particularly a veteran or someone not immediately expected to be capable of programming.
senses.example: Terry wrote that module? I didn't know she was a hack too!
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: An onomatopoeia for coughing.

core.definition: To tolerate or cope with something difficult or unpleasant, usually in the phrase 'can't hack it' or 'can't hack this'.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, flat æ vowel, as in 'cat', and a hard, unaspirated k at the end. Do not add a vowel after the k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it suggests enduring something hard, often with a hint of doubt about whether someone will succeed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hack it' mostly in speech, to say whether someone can handle a job, a schedule, or a climate. In tech, 'hack' also means a quick, workable code fix, and 'a life hack' is a clever shortcut for everyday tasks. Avoid it in formal writing, where 'cope with' or 'tolerate' fits better.

distinctions.note: 'Cope with' is neutral and works in any register; 'hack' is informal and emphasizes getting through something hard.
'Tolerate' is formal and suggests putting up with something one dislikes; 'hack it' is casual and often used about jobs or conditions.
'Hack it' can also mean to succeed, as in 'She could hack it as a surgeon,' so context decides the meaning.

examples.everyday: I love this city, but I honestly can't hack another winter here.
examples.professional: The on-call rotation is brutal, and I'm not sure I can hack it for another six months.
examples.analytical: Whether a person can hack a life of constant uncertainty depends less on private virtue than on the structures that support them.

nuance.analogy: Like a dull axe, it gets the job done only through effort and grit.
nuance.etymology: From Old English haccian, 'to chop'; the informal 'cope' and computing senses developed later.
common_mistakes: Using 'hack' in formal writing where 'tolerate' or 'cope with' is better
Confusing 'hack it' (succeed or cope) with 'hack into' (break into a computer system)

hack.etymology: From Middle English *hacken*, *hakken*, from Old English **haccian* (“to hack”), from **hakkōn*, from Proto-Germanic **hakkōną* (“to chop; hoe; hew”), from Proto-Indo-European **keg-*, **keng-* (“to be sharp; peg; hook; handle”).

senses.definition: To enjoy oneself; to experience enjoyable activities.
senses.example: Blondes have more fun.

senses.definition: Used to wish somebody a good and enjoyable time when they are about to do something.
senses.example: Her coworkers yelled 'Had fun!' as she headed out for the weekend ski trip.

core.definition: To enjoy oneself or take pleasure in an activity, such as a party, trip, game, or outing.

pronunciation.tip: 'Had' is weak and reduces to 'uh' or 'hud' in fast speech, while 'fun' takes the stress. Use a short, relaxed u in 'fun', not a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual; it suggests lighthearted enjoyment and is especially common with children, parties, and trips.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'had fun' constantly for kids, parties, games, and outings, and it is friendly and natural in conversation. Adults often prefer 'had a great time' in more polished settings. 'Have fun!' is a common goodbye, and it can be sarcastic when someone is facing an unpleasant task, as in 'Have fun with that report.'

distinctions.note: 'Had a good time' describes the overall experience, while 'had fun' emphasizes playful enjoyment of an activity.
'Enjoyed' is more formal and can apply to a specific thing, as in 'I enjoyed the lecture'; 'had fun' is casual and lighter.
'Funny' means amusing or strange, not enjoyable, so 'had a funny time' does not mean 'had fun'.

examples.everyday: We had so much fun at the lake last weekend, the kids didn't want to leave.
examples.professional: We had fun building the prototype, even though the deadline was tight.
examples.analytical: Huizinga argued that play is a serious human activity, though we often describe it as merely having fun.

common_mistakes: Confusing 'fun' with 'funny', as in saying 'I had funny' when you mean 'had fun'
Saying 'had the fun' instead of 'had fun'

core.definition: A wife of King David and the mother of his son Adonijah, mentioned in the books of Samuel and Chronicles.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAG. The final 'th' is voiceless, like the 'th' in 'bath', and the last syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a biblical name with no strong emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly know Haggith from Bible reading or study, and the name is rare outside that context. In a conversation about David's family, people usually mention Adonijah alongside her.

examples.everyday: In Bible study we noticed that Haggith is only mentioned briefly, but she was the mother of Adonijah.
examples.professional: When we indexed David's family for the study guide, we listed Haggith under the wives who bore his sons.
examples.analytical: The brief notice of Haggith in the genealogies is significant for understanding the rivalry over succession between Adonijah and Solomon.

nuance.analogy: Like a name in the family tree whose role is quiet but whose son later plays a major part in the story.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name, of uncertain meaning, borne by one of David's wives.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name as HAG-eeth, with a long 'ee' ending.
Confusing her with Hagar, the mother of Ishmael.
nuance.biblical_note: Haggith was one of David's wives in Hebron and the mother of his son Adonijah. 2 Samuel 3:4 lists her among the mothers of David's sons. 1 Chronicles 3:2 repeats the same information. 1 Kings 1:5-11 describes Adonijah's attempt to claim the throne before Solomon.

senses.definition: Clipping of half bathroom.
senses.example: We only have one full bath, so we added a half bath downstairs.

core.definition: A small bathroom with a toilet and sink but no shower or bathtub.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HALF, with a lighter stress on bath, and the th in bath is unvoiced. The first vowel is the short a of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term used in home descriptions and everyday talk about a house.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use half bath mostly in real estate listings and home conversations for a toilet-and-sink room, often near the living area. Guests may simply ask where the bathroom is. Powder room is a more polite or upscale term for the same kind of room, and half-bathroom is the fuller form.

distinctions.note: Powder room is a polite, slightly upscale term for the same kind of room, while half bath is more common in listings.
A full bath includes a shower or tub as well as a toilet and sink.
A three-quarter bath has a toilet, sink, and shower but no tub.

examples.everyday: The downstairs half bath is right past the kitchen if you need it.
examples.professional: The renovation will convert the hall closet into a half bath, which adds value without major plumbing work.
examples.analytical: A half bath separates guest use from the private family bathrooms, which is one reason real estate listings describe it carefully.

nuance.analogy: A half bath is like a studio apartment of bathrooms: it has the essentials but none of the extras.
nuance.etymology: From half plus bath; in this compound, half means partial, lacking a shower or tub.
common_mistakes: Thinking half bath means a bathroom of half size, when it means a bathroom without a shower or tub.
Giving both words equal stress instead of putting the main stress on HALF.

senses.definition: Absurd, foolish or stupid.
Frivolous and silly; featherbrained or scatterbrained; stupid.
senses.example: His hare-brained scheme to sell rowboats in the desert collapsed within a week.

core.definition: Absurd, foolish or reckless, describing an idea or plan that is unlikely to work or is poorly thought out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HAIR, which sounds like the word hair, not like the animal's pronunciation of the vowel. The final syllable is a single sound 'd' after 'braynd'. The word is spelled with a hyphen and pronounced as one unit.

nuance.connotation: Negative, mildly dismissive. It criticizes an idea or person as silly or impractical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hare-brained in casual talk to criticize a plan, scheme or idea, often with some humor. It can describe a person, but it is more often used for ideas. It sounds slightly old-fashioned, so it works well in conversation with friends or colleagues but may sound harsh in formal settings.

distinctions.note: Crazy can describe mental illness or wild behavior; hare-brained focuses on foolish, impractical ideas.
Scatterbrained describes someone forgetful or unfocused; hare-brained describes someone or something silly and unwise.
Absurd is more formal and logical in tone; hare-brained is informal and folksy.

examples.everyday: Don't listen to his hare-brained scheme to sell the car and buy a food truck.
examples.professional: The proposal to rebuild the whole pipeline in two weeks was hare-brained, so we rejected it.
examples.analytical: The critic dismissed the theory as hare-brained, but its central premise anticipates later work on cognitive bias.

nuance.analogy: A hare-brained scheme is like a boat built without a keel: it may look exciting at the dock, but it will not survive the first real wave.
nuance.etymology: From hare (the animal, thought to be excitable) plus brained (having a brain of a certain kind), a figure of speech for wild or foolish thinking.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like the animal's sound 'hair-brained' with a long a in both halves; the first part is hare, pronounced HAIR.
Using it for a person's serious illness or disability, which is offensive and inaccurate.

senses.definition: A male professional killer or gunman.
senses.example: The crime lord dispatched his favorite hatchet man to make sure the witness would not testify.

senses.definition: A male who carries out brutal and unpleasant duties on behalf of another, such as firing dead wood employees.
senses.example: After the layoffs, he gained a reputation as a hatchet man and ended up eating lunches alone.

senses.definition: A male hatchet-wielding participant in a Chinese-American tong war.
senses.example: In the 1920s, a hatchet man from the rival tong stalked the alley, hunting his enemies.

core.definition: A person paid to do the harsh or unpleasant work for a boss, such as firing employees or attacking opponents.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on MAN, with a lighter stress on HATCH. The 'man' uses the short a of 'cat', and the 'et' in hatchet is unstressed, so don't say 'hatch-ett'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies someone who carries out ruthless or unpleasant tasks for others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hatchet man for someone who handles dirty work, such as an executive who delivers layoffs or a political operative who attacks rivals. It is informal and can sound insulting, so use it carefully about colleagues. The word is gendered, but it is often used for women too; 'enforcer' is a neutral alternative.

distinctions.note: Enforcer is neutral and can mean someone who makes rules obeyed; hatchet man usually implies harsh, unpleasant tasks such as firings or attacks.
A hit man is a paid killer; a hatchet man does harsh but usually legal work, though the term can echo violence.
A yes man agrees with everyone to please the boss; a hatchet man actively carries out the boss's difficult orders.

examples.everyday: My uncle says he's basically the hatchet man at his company, the one who has to deliver the layoff news.
examples.professional: I'm not going to be the hatchet man on this reorg; if layoffs happen, they should come from the VP.
examples.analytical: The political scientist argued that party leaders often send a hatchet man into a primary so that their own hands stay clean.

nuance.analogy: A hatchet man is like a demolition specialist hired to clear a site so the builders can start: necessary, unpleasant, and remembered.
nuance.etymology: From hatchet, a small axe, plus man; the figurative sense grew from the older meaning of a hired killer.
common_mistakes: Taking it literally as a killer; in everyday American speech it usually means someone who does harsh but legal work.
Using hatchet man as a formal job title; it is an informal description, not an HR term.

senses.definition: Coastal land that juts into the sea.
The unplowed boundary of a field.
senses.example: The tractor turned at the headland, leaving the unplowed strip along the field's edge.

core.definition: A high piece of land that juts out into the sea or a lake; a cape or promontory.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HED. The final syllable is reduced to a schwa, so it sounds like 'lund,' not 'land.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, often evocative in writing.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, headland appears mainly in literature, maps, and geographic writing. In everyday speech, Americans more often say point, cape, or bluff. The word is more common in British English. Do not use it for the head of a river or for a person's head; it refers only to land.

distinctions.note: Cape is the common American name for a named point of land; headland is more general and literary.
A bluff is a steep cliff face, while a headland may be low and sloping.

examples.everyday: We hiked out to the headland to watch the sunset over the ocean.
examples.professional: The survey crew marked the headland as a key boundary for the coastal access route.
examples.analytical: The poet uses the headland as an image of a threshold between the known land and the unknown sea.

nuance.analogy: Like a finger of land pointing into the water, a headland reaches out from the shore.
nuance.etymology: From head, in the sense of a projecting point, plus land.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable with a full vowel, as in 'HED-land.'
Using headland to mean a leader or the head of an organization.

headland.etymology: From Middle English *hedelond*, *hedelonde*, from Old English *hēafodland*, *hafudland* (“boundary, headland”), equivalent to *head* + *land*.

senses.definition: The state of being free from physical or psychological disease, illness, or malfunction; wellness.
senses.example: Her mental health is really affected by stressful environments.

senses.definition: A state of well-being or balance, often physical but sometimes also mental and social; the overall level of function of an organism from the cellular (micro) level to the social (macro) level.
senses.example: The directors are concerned about the financial health of the project.

senses.definition: Physical condition.
A toast to prosperity.
The amount of damage an in-game entity can withstand before it is killed, destroyed or defeated.
senses.example: The enemies on this level have a lot of health.

core.definition: The condition of your body and mind, and whether you are free from illness or disease.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable ending in a voiceless th, as in thin. Learners often add a vowel between the l and th, or drop the t, so keep the cluster together.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Good health is a valued goal, and talking about health is normal and polite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say good health, in good health, or mental health, and they ask How's your health? in more formal settings. The toast To your health! is common. Americans write health care or healthcare for medical services. They say I'm healthy or I'm in good health, but not I'm in healthy.

distinctions.note: Fitness refers to physical strength and the ability to exercise, while health is a broader state of body and mind.
Wellness is a broader lifestyle term often used in marketing, while health is the basic condition of being free from illness.
Well-being covers happiness and overall life satisfaction, which is broader than physical or mental health.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to take better care of my health, so I walk every morning before work.
examples.professional: Our team owns the health of the payments service, including alerts, uptime, and error rates.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers treat health as a norm of human flourishing, though defining it precisely remains contested.

nuance.analogy: Health is like a bridge in good repair: you rarely think about it until a crack appears.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hǣlth, from the same root as whole and heal.
common_mistakes: Saying I'm in healthy instead of I'm in good health or I'm healthy.
Dropping the t or adding a vowel after the l, as in hel-uth.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses several words that overlap with health, including Hebrew shalom, meaning peace or wholeness, and Greek hygiaino, meaning to be sound or healthy. Third John 1:2 expresses a prayer that a person may be in health, as it goes well with the soul. Proverbs 3:8 promises that trusting God brings healing to the body and refreshment to the bones. Luke 5:31 uses the Greek word hygiainontes for those who are well.

senses.definition: A heliotrope (surveying instrument).

core.definition: A surveying instrument that uses a mirror to reflect sunlight toward a distant point so surveyors can sight it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEE. The final syllable is an open 'ahs' in American speech, not 'ee-us'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American surveying the usual term is heliotrope, and helios is rare, appearing mostly in dictionaries and older surveying texts. Its best-known use is as the name of the Greek sun god Helios. You will seldom hear it in modern US fieldwork, so learn it as a reference word.

distinctions.note: Heliotrope is the common modern name for this surveying instrument in the United States; helios is a rarer synonym.
A heliograph is a device for sending signals by flashing sunlight in code, while a helios is used to mark a precise direction for surveying.

examples.everyday: The surveyor squinted at the far hill and said he'd flash the helios once the sun came out.
examples.professional: Before GPS, our crew set a helios on the ridge to sight control points across the valley.
examples.analytical: The helios turned a sunbeam into a precise sighting line, which made long-distance triangulation possible in clear weather.

nuance.analogy: It works like a pocket mirror on a sunny day, but aimed with great precision at a faraway target.
nuance.etymology: From Greek helios, sun.
common_mistakes: Confusing helios with the sun god Helios, which is correct only in mythology contexts.
Saying the final syllable as 'ee-us', which is not the American pronunciation.

core.definition: In the Bible, the father of Eliab, the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during the wilderness census.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HEE, and end with a short, clear o-n. Do not stretch the final vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see this name only in Bible study or in Scripture readings about the tribes of Israel. It is not used as a personal name today.

examples.everyday: During our Bible reading, we noticed the name Helon appears only as the father of Eliab.
examples.professional: In the lesson on the wilderness census, I pointed out that Helon is mentioned in connection with the tribe of Zebulun.
examples.analytical: The genealogical notice of Helon in Numbers 1:9 functions to identify Eliab's tribal authority within the census structure.

nuance.analogy: Helon is like a footnote in a family record: his name appears only to explain who his son was.
common_mistakes: Confusing Helon with Hilkiah or other similar names.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Helon is named in Numbers 1:9 as the father of Eliab, the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during the census in the wilderness of Sinai. Eliab reappears in Numbers 2:7 and 7:24, where he leads offerings for Zebulun. Helon himself has no independent story, and his role is to identify his son's tribal authority.

senses.definition: Pertaining to hendiadys.

core.definition: Relating to hendiadys, a figure of speech in which two nouns joined by 'and' express a single idea.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the 'ad' syllable, the third one. The 'dy' is pronounced like the word 'die'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hendiadic almost only in literary criticism, rhetoric and biblical or classical studies. It describes phrases where 'X and Y' means 'X-ish Y', as in 'with fire and sword' meaning 'with a fiery sword'. You will not need it in everyday talk, but it may appear in a seminar or scholarly article.

distinctions.note: Hendiadys is the noun for the figure of speech; hendiadic is the adjective for things relating to it.
Tautology is needless repetition; hendiadys uses two words to express one idea, and the pair is not redundant.

examples.professional: When you edit the manual, keep the hendiadic phrasing, because splitting it into two instructions changes the meaning.
examples.analytical: A hendiadic reading of the phrase treats the two nouns as a single image rather than two separate qualities.

nuance.analogy: Like a pair of scissors whose two blades make one cut, a hendiadic pair works together to express one idea.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hen dia dyoin, meaning one through two, from hen (one), dia (through) and dyoin (two).
common_mistakes: Calling any pair of nouns joined by 'and' hendiadic; the figure requires that the two words express one idea.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'HEN-dy-ad-ik'.

senses.definition: Left out of water, stranded on a beach, or in the stocks for repair, or in dry dock.
senses.example: After the tide went out, the fishing boat sat high and dry on the sand.

senses.definition: Abandoned, stranded, helpless.
senses.example: Once the partners left, the small startup was high and dry without any funding.

senses.definition: Associated with the high church (the Church of England and other Anglican traditions, in reference to their "high" political position in England and "dry" and austere mode of worship), as opposed to the "low and slow" Evangelical party and the "broad and shallow" Broad Church.
senses.example: Her grandmother's parish was high and dry, with formal liturgy and no guitars.

senses.definition: With no condiments.
senses.example: The chef served the plain grilled salmon high and dry, without sauce or lemon.

core.definition: Left alone and without help, or stuck in a difficult position with no way to get out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DRY, and 'and' is reduced to 'uhnd' in normal speech. The 'r' in 'dry' is American and clearly pronounced, so avoid a flat 'dry' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing someone who has been abandoned or left in trouble.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression in everyday speech about being left without support, such as when a friend cancels plans at the last minute. A natural reply is 'Oh no, I'm sorry, I'll help you find another ride.' It is informal, so avoid it in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Stranded means unable to leave a place; high and dry means left without help, which can apply to people in any situation.
Left behind is neutral and can mean simply not taken; high and dry suggests a more serious abandonment or trouble.
In the lurch is a near synonym that also means left in a difficult spot, but it is slightly more old-fashioned.

collocations: high and dry on the highway

examples.everyday: My roommate canceled our dinner plans at the last minute and left me high and dry.
examples.professional: When the vendor pulled out of the project, our team was left high and dry with two weeks to deliver.
examples.analytical: The reform left many clergy high and dry, deprived of their old patronage without any clear new role in the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat pulled onto sand when the tide goes out, you are stuck and cannot move until someone comes to help.
nuance.etymology: From the nautical image of a ship left stranded on dry land when the water falls away.
common_mistakes: Using 'high and dry' only for physical objects; in American speech it is most often used for people left in trouble.
Saying 'high and dry' without the word 'and', which is needed in the fixed phrase.

conversation.text: The contractor quit and left us high and dry.
When the vendor went out of business, we were left high and dry.
My ride canceled and left me high and dry at the airport.

senses.definition: Synonym of pitch (“an American trick-taking card game”).

core.definition: Another name for Pitch, an American trick-taking card game in which points come from the high, low, and jack of trump.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on JACK, with lighter stress on 'high' and 'low.' The vowel in 'jack' is the short 'a' of 'cat,' not the 'ah' of 'father.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a playful term from card-playing culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say 'Pitch' for the game and use 'high-low-jack' for the points, especially in parts of the Midwest and the Pacific Northwest. It appears in casual invitations, such as 'Want to play some high-low-jack?' Players often say the names of the points when scoring.

distinctions.note: Pitch is the usual name for the game, while high-low-jack refers to the scoring points and is used in some regions as another name for the game.
Euchre is a different trick-taking game that uses special bower cards, while pitch uses only the trump suit's high, low, and jack.
Bridge is a partnership game with bidding and contracts, while high-low-jack is a simpler trick-taking game.

examples.everyday: Grandpa taught us to play high-low-jack on rainy afternoons at the lake.
examples.professional: For the team offsite, we'll play some high-low-jack after the workshop, so bring your best bluffing face.
examples.analytical: Scoring in high-low-jack rewards control of trump, showing how small rules can shape the strategy of a whole game.

nuance.analogy: Like a scoreboard where only three moments count, so every trick matters.
nuance.etymology: Named for the three trump cards that score in the game: the high, the low, and the jack.
common_mistakes: Treating high-low-jack as a separate game from pitch when it is often just another name for it.
Pronouncing 'jack' with the vowel of 'father' instead of the short vowel of 'cat.'

senses.definition: To depend on; to be contingent upon.
senses.example: The success of this plan hinges upon his approval.

core.definition: To depend entirely on something, so that a result or decision is determined by it.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the g in 'hinge' as the 'j' sound, so it sounds like 'hinj'. Stress the particle 'on' because this is a phrasal verb, and say 'AHN' with an open 'ah' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes dependence without judging whether the outcome is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hinge on' in news, business and everyday discussion of decisions, often in the pattern 'everything hinges on'. 'Hinge upon' is also used, but 'hinge on' is more common in American speech. A natural reply is simply to ask what the key factor is.

distinctions.note: Depend on is general and neutral, while hinge on suggests that one crucial factor controls the outcome.
Hang on is more casual and can mean wait or hold tight, so it is not the best choice for a decision that depends on a factor.
Rest on suggests a foundation or base, while hinge on suggests a turning point that determines the result.

examples.everyday: Our vacation plans hinge on whether the car gets fixed this week.
examples.professional: Our launch date hinges on whether the vendor delivers the data feed by Friday.
examples.analytical: The argument hinges on whether moral obligation can exist without a prior acknowledgment of divine authority.

nuance.analogy: A hinge is the small joint a door swings on, so an outcome that hinges on one factor swings with it.
nuance.etymology: From the noun hinge, a joint on which a door or lid turns, related to hang.
common_mistakes: Using 'hinge from' or 'hinge to' instead of 'hinge on'.
Stressing 'hinge' as the main word, when the stronger stress is usually on 'on'.

senses.definition: A clue.
senses.example: I needed a hint to complete the crossword.

senses.definition: An implicit suggestion that avoids a direct statement.
senses.example: He gave me a hint that my breath smelt.

senses.definition: A small, barely detectable amount.
senses.example: There was a hint of irony in his voice.

senses.definition: Information in a computer-based font that suggests how the outlines of the font's glyphs should be distorted in order to produce, at specific sizes, a visually appealing pixel-based rendering; an instance of hinting.
senses.example: This font does not scale well to small sizes; the hints for the 10-point letter 'g' still need work.

senses.definition: An instruction to the database engine as to how a query should be executed, for example whether to use an index or not.
senses.example: The query hint told the database engine to skip the full table scan.

senses.definition: To imply without a direct statement; to provide a clue.
senses.example: She hinted at the possibility of a recount of the votes.

senses.definition: To bring to mind by a slight mention or remote allusion; to suggest in an indirect manner.
senses.example: to hint a suspicion

senses.definition: To develop and add hints to a font.
senses.example: The typographer worked all day on hinting her new font so it would look good on computer screens.

senses.definition: Signifies that something previously said should be taken as a hint or heeded closely.
senses.example: And yes, as long as you are being a good coder and engaging in safe practices, nothing should go wrong. (Hint, hint.)

core.definition: A small clue or indirect suggestion that helps someone understand something without saying it directly.

pronunciation.tip: It is one short syllable with a short i, like 'sit'. Pronounce the final nt clearly and do not make the vowel a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be friendly or playful, but it can feel pushy when someone drops hints to get what they want.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often 'drop a hint' when they want something but do not want to ask directly. People say 'Did you get the hint?' or 'Take the hint' when they want someone to understand. A natural reply is 'Got it' or 'Sorry, I missed the hint'.

distinctions.note: A clue is a stronger and more useful piece of evidence for solving a problem, while a hint is often a light, indirect suggestion.
A suggestion is a more direct proposal, while a hint is more indirect and often less explicit.
A tip is practical advice, often informal, while a hint suggests something unstated.

examples.everyday: My sister dropped a hint that she wanted a new bike for her birthday.
examples.professional: The quarterly report gives a hint that churn is rising, but the data isn't conclusive yet.
examples.analytical: Her footnote offers a hint of the argument she never develops in the main text.

nuance.analogy: A hint is like a light left on in a window: it tells you someone is home without telling you who.
nuance.etymology: Uncertain; possibly from Middle English hent, to seize or grasp.
common_mistakes: Using hint for direct instructions, when a hint is always indirect.
Confusing 'hint at' with 'hint to'; the usual phrase is 'hint at'.

hint.etymology: From Middle English *hinten*, *hynten*, variant of *henten* (“to lay hold of, catch”), from Old English *hentan* (“to seize, grasp”), from **hantijan*, from Proto-Germanic **hantijaną*.

senses.definition: (An instance of) meaningless nonsense with an outward appearance of being impressive and legitimate.
(An instance of) excessively contrived, hackneyed, or sentimental material in a film, television program, theater production, etc.
senses.example: The screenplay was full of hokum, with a dying dog and a miraculous last-minute rescue.

senses.definition: A film, television program, theater production, etc. containing excessively contrived, hackneyed, or sentimental material.
senses.example: We walked out of the hokum after twenty minutes, tired of the tearful speeches.

senses.definition: A genre of blues song or music, often characterized by sexual innuendos or satire.
senses.example: The record collection included a 1920s hokum blues number with suggestive lyrics about a rooster.

core.definition: Meaningless nonsense dressed up to sound impressive or legitimate, or sentimental, contrived material in a film or show.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HOH, and reduce the final syllable to a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'kum' rather than 'kahm'. Keep the first vowel a long 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes something as fake, overwrought or phony.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hokum in movie reviews, sports commentary, and casual talk about speeches or advertising that feel overblown. It sounds a bit old-fashioned and playful, so it fits informal speech and writing rather than formal reports. A natural reply is 'Yeah, that was a lot of hokum' or 'I'm not buying it'.

distinctions.note: Hogwash means foolish talk or nonsense in general; hokum specifically suggests showy, fake emotion or contrived drama.
Schmaltz is excessive sentimentality, especially in music or film; hokum includes that but also covers showy nonsense.
Hokey is an adjective meaning corny or contrived; hokum is the noun for the thing itself.

examples.everyday: That movie was pure hokum, with a dog that cries on cue.
examples.professional: The pitch deck was full of hokum about AI transforming everything overnight, with no metrics to back it up.
examples.analytical: Much of the sermon's rhetoric was hokum, an emotional performance that substituted sentiment for argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie set built from painted cardboard: it looks solid from the audience, but it can't hold any weight.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; it appeared in American English in the early twentieth century, and its source is not clearly established.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'HOH-kahm', with a full second vowel; the ending is weak.
Using it as a formal word in academic writing, where it sounds too informal.

hokum.etymology: first attested as US theater slang, possibly a *hocus-pocus* + *bunkum*.

senses.definition: Wait a minute; stop.
senses.example: Hold it. What did you say his name was?

senses.definition: To wait to urinate or defecate despite present urgency.
senses.example: Can't you hold it until the next gas station?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hold,‎ it.
senses.example: Can you hold it steady while I tighten the screw?

core.definition: Wait a moment or stop what you are doing; said as a short command, often when someone needs a pause.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HOHLD, and 'it' is short and unstressed, like 'ut' in fast speech. Don't stress 'it' or stretch it into 'eet'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds casual and quick, but said sharply it can sound bossy or impatient.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Hold it!' or 'Hold it right there' to stop someone briefly, and it's common in conversation and in movies. In photography, 'Hold it' asks the subject to stay still. Also, 'I can't hold it' means you cannot wait to urinate, a common everyday expression. A natural reply is 'Okay, take your time' or 'Sure, one second.'

distinctions.note: Wait is neutral and works everywhere; hold it is quicker, more informal, and often a command to pause immediately.
Hang on is friendlier and often means wait while I finish something; hold it can sound sharper or more urgent.
Stop means cease completely, while hold it usually asks for a short pause.

collocations: I can't hold it much longer

examples.everyday: Hold it, I'm almost out the door and I left my keys.
examples.professional: Hold it for a second, Dana; let me pull up the dashboard before we merge the branch.
examples.analytical: In discourse analysis, 'hold it' works as a pragmatic interruption that halts a speaker's momentum until the listener can reorient.

nuance.analogy: Like a traffic light turning red for a moment before the cars move again.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hold on it' or 'hold it on' instead of 'hold it'.
Using 'hold it' for a long delay; it normally means a brief pause.
Stressing 'it' so that the phrase sounds strong or angry.

senses.definition: Synonym of stand one's ground.

core.definition: To refuse to give way under pressure or argument, keeping your position firmly in a disagreement or confrontation.

pronunciation.tip: Ground has the ow diphthong, as in 'out', not 'grund'. The possessive 'one's' reduces to 'wuhnz'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests courage and conviction, though it can sound stubborn if the position is wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in debates, negotiations, sports, and neighborhood disputes: 'She held her ground in the meeting.' 'Stand one's ground' is equally common and nearly identical in meaning, and is often used for physical confrontation. A natural reply to someone who stood firm is 'Good for you for not backing down.'

distinctions.note: Essentially the same; stand one's ground is slightly more common for physical or confrontational situations, while hold one's ground fits debates and negotiations.
Stand firm emphasizes steadiness of decision; hold one's ground suggests refusing to yield during a dispute.
Dig in suggests entrenching for a long fight and can sound stubborn; hold one's ground is more neutral.

collocations: hold your ground in the negotiation
hold your ground in the argument

examples.everyday: My neighbor kept complaining about the fence, but I held my ground and showed him the survey.
examples.professional: Even when the vendor pushed for a cheaper contract, our team held its ground on the data retention terms.
examples.analytical: A philosopher who holds her ground under objection must show that the premise survives the strongest counterexample, not simply repeat it.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree in a storm that bends a little but keeps its roots planted.
nuance.etymology: From Old English grund, 'bottom, base'; the sense of defending a position comes from holding a physical place.
common_mistakes: Dropping the possessive and saying 'hold ground' instead of 'hold your ground'.
Using 'hold on your ground', which is not a natural phrase.
Assuming the phrase only refers to physical land; it is mostly figurative.

senses.definition: A sharpening stone composed of extra-fine grit used for removing the burr or curl from the blade of a razor or some other edge tool.
senses.example: He used a fine hone to sharpen the razor before shaving.

senses.definition: A machine tool used in the manufacture of precision bores.
senses.example: The machinist used a hone to finish the cylinder bore to exact tolerances.

senses.definition: A kind of swelling in the cheek.
senses.example: The doctor said the hone on his cheek would shrink in a few days.

senses.definition: To sharpen with a hone; to whet.
senses.example: Every morning he honed his kitchen knife on a whetstone before chopping vegetables.

senses.definition: To use a hone to produce a precision bore.
senses.example: The shop honed the engine cylinders to hold a tolerance of a few microns.

senses.definition: To refine (a skill especially) by learning.
To make more acute, intense, or effective.
senses.example: The coach honed the team's defense during practice to make them harder to score against.

senses.definition: To grumble.
senses.example: Stop honing about the weather and help me carry these boxes.

senses.definition: To pine, lament, or long.
senses.example: She honed for her absent sailor, longing for his return every evening at the harbor.

senses.definition: Synonym of alas Used to express sorrow, or grief.
senses.example: Hone, what a sorry tale, the old preacher sighed.

core.definition: To sharpen or refine a skill, ability or plan through steady practice over time.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long o that glides into the n, not a short vowel like 'hon'. Don't confuse it with 'honest' (AH-nist), which has the same first sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes improving through effort and attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hone mainly in the skill sense, as in 'hone your skills' or 'honing a pitch.' It sounds polished in a résumé, a performance review or a meeting. The sharpening-stone sense is rare outside workshops, and the interjection 'alas' is archaic.

distinctions.note: Practice is the activity itself, while hone means practicing with the aim of making a skill sharper and more precise.
Sharpen can be literal or figurative; hone implies a longer, more deliberate refinement of an ability you already have.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to hone my Spanish before our trip to Mexico.
examples.professional: The team will hone the onboarding process over the next two sprints.
examples.analytical: Aristotle suggests that virtue is honed through repeated practice rather than innate talent alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a whetstone putting a fine edge on a knife, repeated practice puts a sharper edge on a skill.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hān, stone; the sharpening-stone sense came first and the skill sense developed later.
common_mistakes: Writing 'hone in on' when you mean 'home in on' (to aim toward a target); 'home in on' is the stricter form, though 'hone in' appears often.
Pronouncing it like 'hon' with a short vowel, which sounds like 'honey' or 'hun'.

hone.etymology: From Middle English *hon* (“whetstone”), from Old English *hān*, from Proto-Germanic **hainō*, from Proto-Indo-European **ḱeh₃i-* (“to sharpen”).

senses.definition: A connection.
senses.example: The plumber came to fix the sewer hookup.

senses.definition: A brief sexual relationship or encounter.
senses.example: He met his two most recent partners at bars, and expressed strong ambivalence and dislike of meeting partners online, but reported half a dozen additional hookups with partners met online.

senses.definition: A sexual partner.
senses.example: The predominant way of finding a hookup or sexual partner would be going online.

core.definition: A connection between things, such as cables, utilities, or devices; in informal slang, a casual sexual encounter or partner.

pronunciation.tip: The noun stresses the first syllable, and the verb phrase 'hook up' stresses the second word. Keep the first vowel short, as in 'book,' and say the second syllable as a weak 'up.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral for technical connections such as a water hookup. In dating or sexual contexts, it is casual, sometimes negative, depending on the situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hookup' for physical connections, like a 'cable hookup' or a 'water hookup' for an RV, very often in home, utility, and tech talk. In personal life, the slang sense is common among young adults and can imply a casual encounter without commitment. Be careful in mixed company: the context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: 'Connection' is the neutral, general word, while 'hookup' is more casual and implies a practical link set up by someone.
A date implies a planned outing with intent to form a relationship, while a hookup suggests something casual and short-term.
A fling is a short romance with some emotional attachment, while a hookup is usually more casual and less emotional.

examples.everyday: The plumber said the water hookup for the new dishwasher is ready, so you can run it tonight.
examples.professional: IT needs to confirm the network hookup in the conference room before the meeting starts.
examples.analytical: The sociologist's study of hookup culture asks how casual sexual norms shape young adults' expectations of commitment.

nuance.analogy: A hookup is like a power strip that connects two things quickly, temporary but useful.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb 'hook up,' which dates to the 19th century, with the noun use following in the 20th century.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the one-word noun 'hookup' with the two-word verb 'hook up' in a sentence.
Using 'hookup' in a formal setting where the sexual slang meaning might be misunderstood.

senses.definition: A location which has a higher temperature or amount of radiation than surrounding areas.
senses.example: Thermal imaging showed a hotspot on the server rack where the cooling fan had failed.

senses.definition: A part of a forest fire which is burning actively.
senses.example: Firefighters contained the hotspots along the ridge before the wind could push flames over it.

senses.definition: The surface manifestation of a plume of molten material that rises from deep in a celestial body's mantle.
senses.example: Geologists think the Hawaiian islands formed above a hotspot where magma rises from deep within the mantle.

senses.definition: An area of high radioactive contamination.
senses.example: Officials cordoned off the hotspot near the reactor, where radiation readings were still dangerously high.

senses.definition: Synonym of heiligenschein (“an optical phenomenon which creates a bright spot around the shadow of the viewer's head, when the surface on which the shadow falls has special optical characteristics”).
senses.example: Walking across the dew-soaked meadow at sunrise, I noticed a hotspot ringing my shadow's head.

senses.definition: An infected lesion in dogs or other furry mammals caused by excessive itching.
senses.example: The vet said the dog's hotspot had grown raw from constant scratching and needed antibiotics.

senses.definition: A place notable for a high level of activity or danger.
senses.example: Downtown has become a hotspot for pickpockets during the crowded summer festivals.

senses.definition: A dangerous place of violent political unrest.
senses.example: The border town became a hotspot of violent protests after the disputed election results.

senses.definition: A lively and entertaining place, such as a nightclub.
senses.example: Everyone says the new jazz club on Fifth is the hotspot for weekend nights.

senses.definition: A part of an application that consumes a significant amount of execution time.
senses.example: The profiler showed that the image-parsing function was the hotspot slowing the whole application down.

senses.definition: A part of a control (“an interactive interface element”) that responds dynamically as a user moves a pointer over it (for example, a part of an image map that contains a hyperlink which can be clicked on with a cursor).
senses.example: When I move the cursor over the map, the hotspot highlights and the link appears.

senses.definition: A location in which Wi-Fi Internet access is available.
Ellipsis of biodiversity hotspot (“a place with a significant level of biodiversity, particularly if the flora and fauna are threatened with loss of their habitat”).
The region of a gene in which there is a higher than normal rate of mutation.
senses.example: The promoter region contains a hotspot where mutations occur far more often than elsewhere in the gene.

core.definition: A place where activity, trouble or demand is concentrated; also a location or device offering wireless internet access.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HOT in this compound noun, while spot is lighter. Do not stress the second word, as in hot-SPOT, which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can mean a popular place (positive) or a trouble spot (negative), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say hotspot for a popular restaurant, bar or tourist destination, and also for a trouble area such as a crime hotspot. In tech talk, your phone's hotspot shares its data connection with a laptop or tablet. A natural exchange is Can you turn on your hotspot? The Wi-Fi here is terrible.

distinctions.note: A hotbed is a place where a dangerous or radical movement grows, while hotspot is broader and covers popular places and Wi-Fi access.
A flashpoint is a place where conflict may suddenly break out, a sharper term used in politics and news.

examples.everyday: That taco truck on Main Street is a hotspot on Friday nights.
examples.professional: Turn on your phone's hotspot so the laptop can reach the server while the office Wi-Fi is down.
examples.analytical: Epidemiologists map infection hotspots to see where transmission clusters and why.

nuance.analogy: Like a bright red dot on a weather map, marking where activity is most intense.
nuance.etymology: From hot (warm) plus spot (place); the wireless sense developed much later.
common_mistakes: Writing hot spot as two words in tech contexts, where hotspot is the standard
Stressing the second word, as in hot-SPOT, which sounds unnatural

senses.definition: The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been split at the end of a line.
senses.example: Put a hyphen between 'well' and 'known' when you use it before a noun.

senses.definition: Something which links two things of greater significance than itself.
senses.example: The museum's new gallery serves as a hyphen between the old wing and the modern library.

senses.definition: An enclosed walkway or passage that connects two buildings.
senses.example: We met under the glass hyphen connecting the two hospital buildings.

senses.definition: Someone who belongs to a marginalized subgroup, and can therefore described by a hyphenated term, such as "German-American", "female-academic", etc.
senses.example: As a German-American, she felt like a hyphen whenever people asked where she was really from.

senses.definition: Used to emphasize the coordinating function usually indicated by the punctuation "-".
(dated) To separate or punctuate with a hyphen; to hyphenate.
senses.example: The editor hyphened every compound adjective in the manuscript before sending it to press.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The short punctuation mark (‐) that joins words in a compound, or shows that a word is split across two lines.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HY. The final syllable is a syllabic n: the tongue touches the ridge behind your teeth and there is no full vowel, so it is not 'HY-fen' with a clear EH sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'hyphen' for the short mark only. The longer marks are the en dash and the em dash, and people often call all of them 'dashes' in everyday speech. American style guides such as Chicago and AP give specific rules for hyphens in compound modifiers, so writers at work often ask whether a hyphen is needed. A casual reply to a question about it is simply 'Yes, with a hyphen' or 'No hyphen.'

distinctions.note: The en dash (–) is about the length of the letter n and shows ranges such as 2019–2021, while the hyphen is shorter and joins words.
The em dash (—) is the longest mark and sets off an interruption or an emphatic aside in a sentence.

collocations: hyphen at the end of a line

examples.everyday: My sister always writes 'T-shirt' with a hyphen, but I think it looks cleaner without one.
examples.professional: Please add a hyphen to 'data-driven' in the title before we send the report.
examples.analytical: The hyphen in 're-cover' versus 'recover' shows how punctuation can carry a meaning that the spelling alone does not.

nuance.analogy: A hyphen is like a stitch that joins two pieces of cloth into a single seam.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin hyphen, from Greek hyphen 'under one', meaning 'together as one'.
common_mistakes: Using a hyphen where an en dash is needed, for example in number ranges such as 2019-2021 instead of 2019–2021.
Saying 'hyphen' for the em dash, which Americans normally call a dash.

hyphen.etymology: Late Latin *hyphen*, from Ancient Greek *ῠ̔φέν* (“in one, as a single word”), of *ῠ̔φ’ ἕν* (“under one”), from *ῠ̔πο-* + *ἕν*, neuter of *εἷς* (“one”).

senses.definition: Offering to come get someone in your car at a set time.
senses.example: Hey, I'll pick you up at seven on Saturday for the concert.

core.definition: I'll drive to your location and collect you in my car at seven o'clock.

pronunciation.respelling: ile pik yoo up at SEH-vun
pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEH in seven, and the particle up is weak in this IPA. In speech, 'pick you up' often sounds like 'pi-kyoo-UP,' so the particle carries a light stress. The final -en is a syllabic n, so it sounds like 'SEH-vun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It signals help and reliability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when arranging a ride, a date, or a trip with friends or family. It is very common in everyday life and suits both casual and polite situations. A natural reply is 'Sounds good, see you then' or 'Perfect, I'll be ready.'

distinctions.vs: I'll come get you at seven.
distinctions.note: Nearly identical, and very common in American speech. 'Come get you' is slightly more casual.
Emphasizes the driving, and can imply you are taking them somewhere rather than collecting them from home.

collocations: pick you up from the airport
I'll swing by and pick you up

examples.everyday: Don't worry about parking, I'll pick you up at seven and we can drive together.
examples.professional: Since the office is across town, I'll pick you up at seven for the client dinner.
examples.analytical: The offer 'I'll pick you up at seven' implies a plan with a specific time, a shared location, and a commitment that makes the event more reliable.

nuance.analogy: Like a taxi with a pre-set pickup time, the arrangement is fixed so both people know when to be ready.
nuance.etymology: Pick comes from Middle English pikken, meaning to pluck or pull.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'll pick you at seven' without 'up,' which means something different.
Saying 'pick up you' with the wrong word order instead of 'pick you up.'

conversation.text: I'll pick you up at seven, so be ready out front.

senses.definition: A person who imitates or apes another.

core.definition: A person who copies or imitates another person, often in a way that seems less original or sincere.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is the American 'er' sound, a rhotic r, with no hard 't' sound.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative, suggesting someone who copies rather than creates, though it can be neutral when describing disciples who follow a model.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say imitator when talking about a person who copies a famous person's style or behavior, often in entertainment or fashion, as in 'a Sinatra imitator.' In friendly talk, people more often say 'copycat' or 'impersonator.' In religious speech, imitator can be used positively for someone who follows a good example.

distinctions.note: An impersonator pretends to be a specific person, often for entertainment, while an imitator may just copy a style.
Copycat is informal and usually negative, suggesting someone who copies for advantage.

examples.everyday: My friend is a great imitator, and she can do the voice of every teacher we had.
examples.professional: We need originators, not just imitators, on the design team if we want to stand out.
examples.analytical: Paul calls the Thessalonians imitators of the Lord and of the churches of Judea, showing faith in action.

nuance.analogy: An imitator is like a tracing pad: it reproduces the lines of an original but does not draw its own.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imitator, from imitari, to imitate.
common_mistakes: Using 'imitator' for an impersonator who pretends to be a specific person; the stronger word for that is impersonator.
Saying 'imitater', which is a spelling error for imitator.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is mimetes, imitator. In 1 Corinthians 4:16 Paul asks believers to be imitators of him, and 1 Thessalonians 1:6 says they became imitators of Paul and the Lord. The word expresses following a trusted example in faith and conduct.

imitator.etymology: From French *imitateur*, derived from Latin *imitātor*, equivalent to *imitate* + *-or*.

senses.definition: About to happen, occur, or take place very soon, especially of something which won't last long.
senses.example: Dark clouds gathered over the valley, and everyone knew a thunderstorm was imminent.

core.definition: About to happen very soon, especially something that is coming close and may be dangerous or important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a short ih, and the last syllable is a reduced unt, not ent. Do not confuse it with eminent.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or serious, because imminent usually refers to danger, disaster or major change. It can be neutral for good news, such as an imminent announcement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imminent in news, weather warnings, legal writing and business talk: an imminent threat, an imminent decision. In casual speech they more often say about to happen or coming up soon. Saying the rain is imminent sounds slightly formal or dramatic but is natural in weather reports.

distinctions.note: Eminent means famous and respected; imminent means about to happen. The words look alike but mean different things.
Impending is very close to imminent and often used for bad events; imminent is slightly more neutral and more common in technical writing.

examples.everyday: The sky is getting dark and the weather service says a storm is imminent, so let's go inside.
examples.professional: Our monitoring dashboard shows an imminent disk failure, so we need to migrate the data tonight.
examples.analytical: Many theologians argue that the New Testament speaks of an imminent end, yet the delay of that end became a central problem.

nuance.analogy: An imminent event is like a car at the top of a hill: it has already started rolling and will arrive at the bottom soon.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imminens, present participle of imminere, to overhang, from in- (on) and minere (to jut).
common_mistakes: Confusing imminent with eminent, which means famous or distinguished.
Using imminent for something in the distant future; it must be close in time.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of nearness is expressed by the Greek word engys (ἐγγύς), meaning near or at hand. Philippians 4:5 says the Lord is at hand, encouraging believers to live with gentleness because the Lord's presence is near. James 5:8 tells believers to establish their hearts because the coming of the Lord is at hand. Romans 13:12 says the night is far gone and the day is at hand, urging believers to put off the works of darkness.

imminent.etymology: From the present participle of Latin *imminēre* (“to overhang”), from *mineō*, related to *minae* (English *menace*) and *mons* (English *mount*).

senses.definition: To make someone or something immune to something.
senses.example: Years of exposure to the local bacteria seem to have immunized him against the strain.

senses.definition: To inoculate someone, and thus produce immunity from a disease.
senses.example: The clinic will immunize all second graders against measles this Thursday morning.

core.definition: To protect a person or animal against a disease by giving them a vaccine or other treatment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, IM. The middle syllable is a reduced 'yuh', and the final -ize sounds like 'nyze' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Positive and neutral; it describes a protective, responsible action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'immunize' in health offices, schools and news reports about vaccination campaigns. The American spelling is 'immunize', while British English uses 'immunise'. In casual talk, people often say 'get shots' or 'get vaccinated' instead.

distinctions.note: Vaccinate names the act of giving a vaccine; immunize emphasizes the protection that results, though the two are often interchangeable in US health contexts.

examples.everyday: Did the doctor say the kids are fully immunized before school starts?
examples.professional: We plan to immunize all staff before the winter season to reduce absences.
examples.analytical: A state can immunize its population only if citizens trust the institutions that deliver the vaccine.

nuance.analogy: Like giving a building's security staff a photo of the intruder before anyone breaks in.
nuance.etymology: From immune plus -ize, to make immune; immune comes from Latin immunis 'exempt'.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'immunise' in American writing.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ih-MYOO-nize'.

senses.definition: The state of being impassive.

core.definition: The quality of showing no visible emotion or reaction, even under stress or provocation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PASS. The -ive ending is reduced to a short 'iv' and the final -ness is a short 'nus'. Do not insert an extra vowel between the v and the n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it can suggest admirable composure or cold detachment, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'poker face' or 'stone face' in casual speech, and use impassive as the adjective. Impassiveness is a formal noun, typical in news writing, reviews, or descriptions of judges, officers, or interviewers. It can be praise, as in 'his impassiveness under pressure'.

distinctions.note: Calmness describes a peaceful inner state; impassiveness describes a visible lack of reaction, which may hide strong feelings.
Indifference means not caring; impassiveness may be outward composure that hides deep care.

examples.everyday: I admire his impassiveness when the kids are screaming, but honestly I think he is just tired.
examples.professional: Her impassiveness during the performance review made it hard to know how she felt about the feedback.
examples.analytical: Stoic writers praised impassiveness as a virtue, yet the question remains whether it expresses a well-ordered emotional life or its absence.

nuance.analogy: Like a lake under a windless sky: the surface shows nothing, though the depths may be moving.
nuance.etymology: From impassive plus -ness; impassive comes from Late Latin impassivus, from in- ('not') plus passivus ('capable of suffering').
common_mistakes: Using impassiveness as an adjective; the adjective is impassive.
Confusing it with passivity, which means not taking initiative rather than not showing emotion.

senses.definition: In an impersonal manner.
senses.example: use a verb impersonally

core.definition: In a detached or businesslike way that does not show personal feeling or relate to a particular person.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUR, and the second and third syllables reduce to schwa. The ending is '-ly', pronounced 'lee', with only one L sound, not 'lee' with a double L.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually describes communication or treatment that feels cold or detached.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb mostly to describe how something was written, delivered, or handled, such as an impersonal notice or an impersonally written report. In everyday conversation, people more often say 'coldly' or 'like a robot' when they want to sound critical.

distinctions.note: Coldly emphasizes unfriendly emotion. Impersonally emphasizes a lack of individual attention or personal connection.
Objectively means based on facts without bias. Impersonally can be neutral like that, but it often suggests a lack of warmth.

examples.everyday: The landlord sent the notice impersonally, with no name at the top, so it felt like spam.
examples.professional: The rejection email was written impersonally, so I'd like to rewrite it with a specific reason.
examples.analytical: The report describes the policy impersonally, as if the people affected had no stories of their own.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign that says 'Please take a number' with no greeting, something handled impersonally treats you as a case, not as a person.
nuance.etymology: From impersonal plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin persona (person, mask).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending with a double L, as 'impersonall-y'.
Using 'impersonally' to mean 'anonymously' when 'anonymously' is the more precise word for hidden authorship.

senses.definition: Not capable of being, or not easily, perturbed, excited, or upset; calm and collected, even under pressure.

core.definition: Calm and collected, not easily upset or excited, even in difficult or stressful situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TUR, the third syllable. The last two syllables are reduced, so say 'buh-buhl' with light vowels, not a strong 'bull'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes admirable calm, though it can sound a little stiff or dramatic in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to describe people who stay calm under pressure, such as a pilot, a surgeon, or a coach. In everyday conversation people more often say 'calm,' 'cool,' or 'unflappable.' It is common in journalism and reviews, and it suits a formal compliment.

distinctions.note: Unflappable is more casual and conversational, while imperturbable sounds more formal and literary.
Calm describes a state at any moment; imperturbable suggests a steady, deep calm that does not break under strain.
Impassive means showing no feeling at all, which can sound cold, while imperturbable is usually a positive quality.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor stayed imperturbable when the storm knocked out the power and the kids were scared.
examples.professional: The client was angry, but our project manager stayed imperturbable and walked everyone through the fix.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's ideal of the good person includes an imperturbable character that does not collapse under fortune's blows.

nuance.analogy: Like a ship's keel that keeps it upright even when the sea is rough.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imperturbabilis, 'not disturbed', from in- 'not' plus perturbare 'to disturb thoroughly'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'im-PUR-tuh-buhl'.
Saying 'imperturbable' with a full final vowel, as in 'bul', instead of a reduced ending.

imperturbable.etymology: From Late Middle English *imperturbable* (“undisturbed; impossible to disturb”), borrowed from Late Latin *imperturbābilis*, from Latin *im-* (variant of *in-*) + Late Latin *perturbabilis* (“perturbable”) (from Latin *perturbō* (“to confuse; to alarm,…

senses.definition: To obtain by asking; to procure upon request.
senses.example: The nonprofit hoped to impetrate a grant from the foundation for its literacy program.

senses.definition: To ask for, demand.
senses.example: The delegates impetrated the release of the prisoners through a formal written demand.

senses.definition: Impetrated.
senses.example: The impetrated pardon arrived only after the governor reviewed the petition.

senses.definition: Obtained by entreaty.
senses.example: The pardon was an impetrated favor, granted only after the family pleaded for mercy.

core.definition: To obtain something by asking or petitioning for it, especially a favor or a grace from a higher authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'IM'. The final 'ate' is a long 'ayt' sound, and the middle vowel is a short 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a rare, learned word, mainly found in theological, legal, or historical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans would not know this word, and it appears mainly in older theology, church history, or legal writing. In everyday speech people say 'ask for', 'request', or 'obtain'. Use it only in formal or scholarly writing, and expect your audience to notice it.

distinctions.note: Request is the everyday word for asking politely; impetrate is rare and specialized, often for asking a higher authority for a favor.
Obtain stresses getting something; impetrate emphasizes the act of asking that gets it.
Petition usually means a formal written appeal to an authority; impetrate is more technical and rarely used.

examples.everyday: I would rather just ask my boss for the afternoon off than try to impetrate it.
examples.professional: Before the audit, the division had to impetrate approval from the regional board, which took three weeks.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians debated whether a saint could impetrate grace on behalf of the living.

nuance.analogy: Like sending a formal letter to the king asking for a pardon rather than just talking to a friend.
nuance.etymology: From Latin impetrare, 'to obtain by request', from in- 'in' plus patrare 'to accomplish'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual synonym for 'ask for' in everyday speech, which sounds stiff.
Confusing it with 'impetuous' or 'impetus', which are different words.

impetrate.etymology: Latin *impetrātus*, perfect passive participle of *impetrō* (see *-ate* and *-ate*), from *in-* + *pātrō* (“to achieve, make happen”).

senses.definition: The act or conduct of an impostor; deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
senses.example: The dealer's imposture collapsed when a jeweler noticed the diamonds were cubic zirconia.

core.definition: Deception in which someone falsely pretends to be another person or to have a false identity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable (-PAHS-). The -ture ending is pronounced 'chur' (tʃɚ) in American English, not 'tyoor', as in 'posture'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies deliberate deception, often with a sense of betrayal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this formal word mainly in writing about fraud, history, or literature, as in 'a literary imposture' or 'a political imposture'. In everyday talk they say 'con', 'scam', 'fake', or 'phony'. For the person, the usual noun is 'impostor', while 'imposture' names the deception itself.

distinctions.note: 'Impostor' names the person who deceives, while 'imposture' names the act or the fraud itself.
'Fraud' is a common legal and everyday term for intentional deception for gain, while 'imposture' stresses pretending to be someone else.
A hoax is a trick played for amusement or to spread a false belief, while 'imposture' implies a false identity or role.

examples.everyday: When the man who claimed to be a lawyer got caught, the whole neighborhood felt cheated by the imposture.
examples.professional: Our security team found that the vendor's certificates were an imposture, so we ended the contract.
examples.analytical: Some historians argue that the supposed letters were an imposture, written later to support a political claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume worn so long that the wearer tries to pass as the real thing, deceiving everyone who looks.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin impostura, 'deception', from impostor, 'deceiver'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'imposture' (the act) with 'impostor' (the person); say 'he is an impostor', not 'he is an imposture'.
Pronouncing the -ture ending as 'tyoor' or stressing the second syllable with a long vowel; say 'im-PAHS-chur'.

imposture.etymology: From Middle French *imposture*, from Late Latin *impostura*, Latin *impostus*.

senses.definition: An integral where at least one of the endpoints is taken as a limit, either to a specific number or to infinity.

core.definition: An integral in which at least one endpoint is infinite or a point where the function is unbounded, handled by taking a limit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PRAH in 'improper' and IN in 'integral.' Americans say 'IN-tuh-gruhl' with a quick, reduced middle vowel, and the 'r' in 'proper' is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: This term is used in calculus and analysis courses in the United States. Students should not confuse 'improper' here with the everyday meaning of 'not proper.' Instructors often say 'improper integral' and then describe the limit they take.

distinctions.note: A proper integral has finite limits and a bounded integrand; an improper integral has an infinite limit or an unbounded integrand.
A definite integral has fixed finite endpoints; an improper integral is a definite integral whose endpoints or integrand break that condition, so it is evaluated as a limit.

collocations: improper integral of the first kind

examples.everyday: My brother is studying calculus, and he keeps talking about improper integrals.
examples.professional: Before we use this estimator, we need to check that the improper integral converges.
examples.analytical: The distribution's normalization depends on whether the improper integral over the real line converges absolutely.

nuance.analogy: Like walking a path that never ends: you measure the distance by seeing where it approaches.
nuance.etymology: 'Improper' from Latin in- 'not' plus proprius 'one's own, proper'; 'integral' from Latin integer 'whole.'
common_mistakes: Thinking 'improper' means the integral is wrong or illegal; it only means the endpoints or integrand require a limit.
Stressing 'integral' on the second syllable (in-TEG-ral) instead of the first.

senses.definition: Naked.

core.definition: Without any clothes on; completely naked. Usually used humorously or euphemistically.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on the GEH syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on awl. The final -er becomes a reduced American r-colored vowel, and the unstressed the reduces to 'thuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It is a light euphemism and can sound jokey, so it is less suitable for serious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in casual talk, often as a joke or to avoid the blunt word 'naked'. It is less common today than it once was, and in medical, legal or formal writing people say 'nude' or 'naked'. A natural reply is simply a laugh or a comment like 'Well, we did not need that image.'

distinctions.note: 'Naked' is the neutral, direct word; 'in the altogether' is a playful euphemism.
'Nude' is common in art, modeling and photography; the phrase is more informal and humorous.

collocations: in the altogether for the photo

examples.everyday: Don't walk into the bathroom, Dad is still in the altogether after his shower.
examples.professional: The clothing-optional resort's guidelines say staff may not enter guest areas while a guest is in the altogether.
examples.analytical: Sartre's account of shame begins with the self caught in the altogether before another's gaze, feeling exposed and objectified.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume taken all the way off: nothing is left on at all.
